For the last century, the standard text of the Greek New Testament has been greatly influenced by the work of B.F. Westcott and F.J.A. Hort. Their 1881 edition, The New Testament in the Original Greek, paved the way for the modern eclectic method and a new standard text that eclipsed the Textus Receptus. Although many heralded this as a necessary corrective, others viewed it as an over-correction, objecting to a methodology that in practice failed to account for the actual history of the text’s transmission. This neglect of transmissional history led modern textual critics to rely on a small number of early manuscripts, often prioritizing a tiny fraction of the total evidence over the overwhelming majority of the tradition. Furthermore, the subjective nature of the eclectic method has, in some instances, resulted in the adoption of individual readings that lack any extant Greek manuscript support.

The historical justification for this shift was the “Lucianic” or “Syrian” recension theory, a concept formalized by Westcott and Hort. This theory claimed that the Byzantine Textform, which comprises the preponderant majority of surviving manuscripts, was the product of a fourth-century effort to standardize the New Testament. As time progressed, however, no historical evidence for such a recension materialized. While the theory has been largely abandoned by modern scholars, its collapse gives rise to a difficult question: If there was no official recension, how did the Byzantine Textform come to dominate the Greek tradition so consistently across such vast geographical distances?

In the absence of a formal recension, the current dominant explanation is the process view, which suggests that the Byzantine Textform arose through a gradual smoothing of the text by scribes over centuries. Yet this theory struggles to account for the sheer ubiquity and coherence of the text across great distances and centuries of decentralized transmission. This internal consistency is further highlighted by the newest text-critical method: the Coherence-Based Genealogical Method (CBGM). While the CBGM has caused the traditional view of other “text-types” to collapse into so-called “clusters” due to blurred boundaries, it has left the Byzantine Textform intact as a clearly identifiable and coherent tradition.

Given the Byzantine text’s unique standing as a distinct and unified Textform, a more organic and reasonable proposition is that the Byzantine Textform exists because it most closely reflects the autographic text of the New Testament. Its geographic distribution and general consistency are the natural byproducts of faithful transmission by generations of scribes. To put it plainly, it was the text used “on the ground” by the largest number of Christians for the longest period of time across the broadest geographical distance.

The Greek New Testament According to the Byzantine Text is a modern presentation of this historic text. While this edition is the work of an independent committee, its main text is aligned with the Robinson-Pierpont 2026 text. A comprehensive list of textual changes made since the Robinson-Pierpont 2018 edition can be found in Appendix A.

In presenting the current version of this text, we have prioritized usability and utility in our volume’s production. It has been our intention to create a resource that would serve the reader for a lifetime of investigation. Consequently, this digital edition is designed to provide a clear, reliable, and accessible format for daily study and use.
A Comparative Resource for the Church

The Greek New Testament According to the Byzantine Text is designed primarily for pastors and students of Scripture. To this end, we have developed an entirely new “edition” apparatus that prioritizes clarity over the complexity of traditional critical editions. Rather than reproducing existing text-critical notes, we have performed our own rigorous digital collations to compare this text directly and comprehensively against eleven landmark Greek New Testament editions.

This apparatus serves as a functional bridge between the Greek text and today’s pulpit. When modern translations differ, the reader can look to the apparatus to see which printed Greek editions support those variations. This allows the student of Scripture to trace the translational differences back to the textual roots of their Greek editions. Additionally, a second apparatus provides extensive early manuscript evidence for fifty significant variant units, allowing the reader to view all available manuscript evidence from the ninth century and prior.

Because we believe this work is an accurate representation of God’s written word, we have placed the entirety of this edition, including the apparatus and introductory material, into the public domain. No permission is required for its use, reproduction, or distribution. Scripture does not belong to any individual or organization; it belongs to the Body of Christ.

We owe a debt of gratitude to the decades of scholarly labor provided by Dr. Maurice A. Robinson and the late William G. Pierpont. Their preservation of the Byzantine Textform provided the essential foundation for this project. We also thank the many contributors who assisted with collation, software development, typesetting, proofreading, and promoting this edition.

We would also like to express sincere appreciation to Robert Adam Boyd, publisher of The Text-Critical Greek New Testament: Byzantine Text, 2022, for his invaluable input. His public domain work served as a catalyst and model for the Edition Apparatus of the present edition. We are especially grateful for his early adoption of the software approach to variant marking, a partnership that led to the significant refinement and perfection of the software used to produce this edition.

Most importantly, we thank Jesus Christ our Lord for the strength to see this four-year project through to its conclusion. Our prayer is that you find this edition a faithful companion in your studies as you seek to glorify God through His Word.

The following Introduction outlines the editorial principles and technical conventions employed in this edition of the Greek New Testament. While the Preface provides the historical and theological rationale for this project, this Introduction serves as a practical guide to the features of the main text and the methodology behind the comparative apparatuses.

The Greek New Testament According to the Byzantine Text provides two detailed lower margin apparatuses: an “Edition” Apparatus and a “Manuscript” Apparatus. Both of the lower margin apparatuses focus primarily on textual variations—differences in wording or word order that may alter the meaning, phrasing, or general character of the text. Minor variations, such as differences in breathing marks, accents, punctuation, and capitalization are generally excluded. Spelling differences (except for movable Nu / final Sigma) are documented for completeness and to reflect the general character of the various Greek New Testament editions.

The Edition Apparatus is designed to orient the reader quickly to notable differences between the main text of this edition and variant readings found in the main text of eleven landmark Greek New Testament editions.

The Manuscript Apparatus lists early manuscript evidence for fifty of the most significant variant units. For a list of the passages containing these variants, see the Manuscript Apparatus Variant Unit Index. The manuscripts cited in the Manuscript Apparatus include all papyri and uncials extant for these fifty units (ninth century and prior), alongside select minuscules through the tenth century.
Manuscripts are cited whenever they are extant for a particular variant unit. For a list of these manuscripts and their accepted dates, see Appendix D of this volume.

While the Byzantine text is not determined strictly based on manuscripts dating to the tenth century or earlier, the Manuscript Apparatus shows that early manuscripts frequently support the Byzantine text in large numbers. While critics of the Byzantine text often argue that the Critical Text is based on the earliest manuscripts, the Manuscript Apparatus shows that the Byzantine text is also well supported among the earliest manuscripts. Unfortunately, critical text apparatuses frequently omit early Byzantine manuscripts from their lists of consistently cited witnesses. The Manuscript Apparatus is intended to make up for such omissions while not ignoring the manuscripts that typically support the Critical Text.
Editions Compared in the Edition Apparatus

The Edition Apparatus compares the main text of this edition against eleven other editions, which are categorized below. Abbreviations used in the apparatus are provided here and in the comprehensive list of abbreviations and bibliographic references.
These editions generally align with the Byzantine textual tradition:
HF The Greek New Testament According to the Majority Text, 2ⁿᵈ ed. (Hodges and Farstad)
PCK The Greek New Testament According to Family 35, 3ʳᵈ ed. (Pickering)
PT The Ecumenical Patriarchal Text of the New Testament (Antoniades, 1912).

These editions share a focus on early manuscripts from the Alexandrian textual cluster, such as Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus. Their methodologies range from “Reasoned Eclecticism,” with roots in the late nineteenth-century work of Westcott and Hort, to the data-driven “Genealogical” models of the twenty-first century.
ECM Editio Critica Maior (applicable only in Mark, Acts, the Catholic Epistles, and Revelation)
TH The Greek New Testament, Produced at Tyndale House, Cambridge (Jongkind and Williams)
WH The New Testament in the Original Greek (Westcott and Hort)

Textus Receptus editions are historically significant, serving as the basis for the King James and New King James versions. Their inclusion allows the reader to observe their precise relationship with the Byzantine tradition, clarifying where the two traditions align, where they diverge, and where Textus Receptus editions differ from one another.
SCR The New Testament in the Original Greek According to the Text Followed in the Authorized Version (Scrivener)
Special Abbreviations in the Edition Apparatus
The Edition Apparatus uses the following abbreviations to represent alternate textual streams (ʀᴘᵐᵍ, ᴇᴄᴍ†), combinations of editions (ᴄᴛ, ɴᴀ, ᴛʀ), or both (ᴄᴛ†):
RPᵐᵍ Robinson and Pierpont’s alternate Byzantine readings.
ECM† Denotes one of multiple possible readings in the ᴇᴄᴍ where the editors did not designate a single primary text. This is referred to as a “split guiding line.”
CT Denotes agreement between all critical text editions (ᴇᴄᴍ [where appropriate], ɴᴀ, ꜱʙʟ, ᴛʜ, ᴡʜ).
CT† Denotes agreement between ɴᴀ, ꜱʙʟ, ᴛʜ, ᴡʜ, and one branch of an ᴇᴄᴍ split guiding line.
NA Denotes agreement between the ɴᴀ²⁷ and ɴᴀ²⁸ editions.
TR Represents agreement between the Scrivener (ꜱᴄʀ) and Stephanus (ꜱᴛ) editions.

In limited instances, the editors note that there are typographical errors in the printed comparison editions. In such cases, the apparatus records the reading according to the apparent intent of the original editors rather than the typographical error in the printed text. A full table of these corrections is provided in Appendix B of this volume.

The main text of this volume is based on the text of The New Testament in the Original Greek: Byzantine Textform 2026 (edited by Maurice A. Robinson and William G. Pierpont). In seven instances, this edition’s main text differs from the 2018 Robinson-Pierpont text (Matt. 22:4 [punctuation], 26:29, Rom. 13:9, Phil. 3:5, Phm. 1:1, Rev. 11:16, Rev. 13:14), and it reflects sixteen changes to their alternate readings. Please refer to Appendix A for a comprehensive list of these changes and readings.

Paragraph divisions in this edition generally follow the pattern established in the Robinson-Pierpont 2005 and 2018 editions. However, the 2005 edition marked every chapter break as a paragraph division, even when contrary to the intent of that edition’s editors (e.g., Mark 9). For this edition, divisions have been reviewed and restored to match the original intent of the Robinson-Pierpont 2005 editors.

The Edition Apparatus details the readings of comparison editions against the main text. Here is an example note from this apparatus, followed by an explanation of the structure and conventions used in the notes:
ᵉ 1:25 τον υιον αυτης τον πρωτοτοκον ¦ ᴄᴛ υιον
Structure and Conventions of a Note
Each note in the Edition Apparatus follows a standard structure:
Main Text: The main text reading from this edition.
Separator: A broken vertical bar (¦) separates the main text reading from alternate readings.
Alternate Readings: The abbreviations of the supporting editions followed by the variant text.
To ensure the apparatus notes remain concise, the following conventions are observed:

Footnote Callers: The note “caller” (a superscript lowercase letter) in the main text immediately precedes the portion of text subject to variation. The number of main text words affected by the variant can be determined by viewing the main text reading in the apparatus note (e.g., τον υιον αυτης τον πρωτοτοκον in the example note above, which shows five words from the main text being replaced by a single word from the ᴄᴛ editions).
Verse Ranges: If the affected main text spans a verse division, the note explicitly states the verse range (e.g., 1:7–8).

Diacritics and Capitalization: Readings generally omit capital letters and diacritics (breathing marks and accents). Diacritics are retained only when necessary to distinguish between words that would otherwise appear identical (e.g., ἕν versus ἐν).

Brackets: Single [ ] and double [[ ]] brackets from comparison editions, including ᴘᴛ small-font text represented here by single brackets, are preserved to reflect those editors’ uncertainty regarding the authenticity of the bracketed passages.

Revelation Numerals: In the Book of Revelation, differences between spelled-out numbers and Greek letters functioning as numerals are not noted if they are textually equivalent. For example, no note is given for Rev. 7:7, where the main text reading δωδεκα is textually equivalent to the ιβʹ reading found in some other editions.
Versification: Significant versification differences within variants, where a word or phrase is assigned to a different verse number by a comparison edition, are noted.
The following conventions appear within variant listings:

Brackets or Chevrons with Edition Abbreviations: When a comparison edition agrees with the main text but encloses that text in brackets or «chevrons», the abbreviation itself is enclosed in the apparatus (e.g., [ᴡʜ], [[ᴇᴄᴍ]], or «ᴘᴛ»). While brackets ([…] or [[…]]) indicate that the editors expressed textual uncertainty, «chevrons» in ᴘᴛ simply reflect its original punctuation without signaling editor doubt. Note that this convention is also used when multiple editions are involved (e.g., [ᴘᴛ ᴡʜ] or [[ꜱʙʟ ᴡʜ]]).

Movable Nu/Sigma: This edition treats movable Nu and final Sigma omissions both as orthographic variations. To maintain a clean and focused apparatus, these orthographic variations are consolidated using parentheses. When a movable or omitted letter is enclosed in parentheses within the apparatus, it indicates that some listed editions include the letter while others do not.

Ellipses: An ellipsis (…) is used to shorten long variants or to indicate that a specific variation occurs multiple times within the cited main text. The ellipsis replaces text that is identical in both the main text and the variant, ensuring that the reader can reconstruct the complete reading.
Latin Descriptors: The Latin descriptors txt (textus) and om. (omittunt) are used to indicate agreement with the main text or the total absence of a word or words, respectively.
These examples from Matthew and Mark demonstrate specific variant conventions mentioned above:
Variation with Ellipses: 1:5 βοοζ … βοοζ ¦ ᴄᴛ βοες … βοες (The critical text editions read βοες in both instances where the main text reads βοοζ).
Bracketed Authority: 1:18 ιησου ¦ [ᴡʜ] (ᴡʜ agrees with the main text wording but encloses the name ιησου in brackets).
Significant Omission: 7:16 ει τις … ακουετω ¦ [[ᴇᴄᴍ]] ¦ ɴᴀ ᴘᴛ ꜱʙʟ ᴛʜ ᴡʜ om. (ᴇᴄᴍ double-brackets the entire phrase, while ɴᴀ ᴘᴛ ꜱʙʟ ᴛʜ ᴡʜ omit the phrase entirely).

Complex Split Readings: 3:31 φωνουντες ¦ ᴇᴄᴍ† txt ¦ ᴄᴛ† καλουντες (One branch of an ᴇᴄᴍ split guiding line agrees with the main text, while the other ᴇᴄᴍ branch agrees with the Critical Text reading καλουντες).

The Manuscript Apparatus lists early manuscript evidence for fifty of the most significant variant units. Here is an example from the Gospel of Matthew, followed by an explanation of how to interpret the data from this apparatus.
When a manuscript has been altered by a scribe later in its history, scholars need to distinguish between the “original” hand and the “correcting” hand.

Superscript Asterisk (*): This indicates the original reading of the manuscript when there are corrections. For example, in Matthew 4:10, C* means the original scribe of Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus omitted (om.) the phrase οπισω μου.

Superscript Numerals (¹, ², ³): These identify specific correctors. For example, in Matthew 4:10, C² refers to the second corrector who made changes to the manuscript. Additionally, the second corrector (C²) of Codex C included the words οπισω μου, which were omitted by the original scribe.

Superscript Lowercase “c” (ᶜ): This stands for “corrector.” It is generally used when there is a known correction, but the specific “number” of the corrector hasn’t been distinguished, or when there is only one significant layer of correction.
Superscript Lowercase “s” (ˢ): Latin supplementum indicates a reading derived from a later addition to a manuscript, such as a replacement for a folio or section of a manuscript.
These symbols deal with the clarity and exactness of the physical manuscript.

Parentheses ( ): Parentheses indicate that a manuscript supports the variant in essence but has a minor orthographic (spelling) difference or a slight variation in word order that doesn’t warrant putting it in a completely different category.

Superscript “vid” (ᵛⁱᵈ): This is an abbreviation for the Latin videtur, which means “it appears.” This is used when a manuscript is damaged, faded, or the ink is smudged. It indicates that based on the visible traces or the amount of space available on the page (lacunae), the manuscript appears to support that specific reading, but not with certainty because the text isn’t perfectly legible.

The work of textual criticism is complex, and many have labored diligently in the field of textual criticism to produce Greek New Testament editions. This volume seeks to make the results of that labor easily accessible for daily use in the work of the church. With the above conventions in mind, the reader is equipped to explore the Byzantine Textform and its relationship to other Greek New Testament editions.

GREEK NEW TESTAMENT COMPARISON EDITION CORRECTIONS

The variant notes in this volume have been made on the basis of the corrections listed below. The corrections in ᴘᴛ and ꜱᴛ are based on other editions of the same basic Greek text. For ʜꜰ, the corrections in Luke 1:36, John 15:13, John 21:7, Romans 16:1, and Hebrews 10:17 are based on the fact that (1) ʜꜰ does not document variants in the apparatus, and (2) these readings have no support among Byzantine manuscripts. The correction in Revelation 9:18 is based on the apparatus, which indicates that Ἀπὸ is the intended reading. The changes in the other verses correct what are clearly typographical errors.
